name: Lena Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior lead at Fernhill, a 700-hectare farm owned by a family company. We grow wheat and sugar beet and finish about 400 beef cattle a year, which means we buy them young and feed them up to sale weight. I start at seven with the cattle team, then I'm out walking crops, checking for disease, and booking contractors. I've got six people reporting to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the planning. Getting beet out of the ground before the frost and the cattle off to market in the same week, and it all works. What wears me out is the phone. Contractors, the agronomist, the bosses, all day. I use a crop disease app now and then, the agronomist put me onto it, and it's decent for a quick check before I call him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool, use it where it works, don't pay silly money for it. That's what I'd tell the other managers at the grain group meeting. I'm not much of a poster online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and a bit easier. Which is fine. I wasn't losing sleep either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep using the disease app, maybe try the one for planning cattle feed if a few other farms say it's good. Keep saving, and Kofi and I would pay a bit more off the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Like a regular Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the disease app now and then. Does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe I'd use it a bit more once the agronomist trusts it. He checks its answers and so far it's right about four times in five. Good enough for a first look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd miss out on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If AI had got really good, the forms would vanish and I'd have more time in the fields. So I'd miss that. But I'd survive.

S0.say: It's a handy tool, so use it where it works and don't pay silly money for it. That's what I'd tell the other managers at the grain group meeting.
S0.think: It means my job's safe and a bit easier, which is fine by me. I wasn't losing sleep over AI either way, so nothing really changes.
S0.do: Keeps using the crop disease app and might try a cattle feed planner if other farms rate it. Keeps saving and pays a bit more off the house with her partner.
S0.feel: Calm, like a regular working day.
S0.quote: He checks its answers and so far it's right about four times in five.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is matter-of-fact. She judges tools by results and waits for others to vouch for them. She'd like AI to take the paperwork off her but isn't upset when it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that adapt will do fine and ones that don't will struggle, same as always. I'd say get your people trained. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. A manager who can run machines and people is worth more. My worry is more the team, and my own patience with learning all the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which robots the bigger farms around us buy and how they get on for a year. Then I'd put a plan to the owners for one or two, probably for weeding beet. I'd do a short course in farm data over the winter, if the company paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit tired at the idea of more systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your six people would this hit hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Mick, who does the beet hoeing and drives the loader. He's 50 and he's good, but he'd tell you himself he hates change. I'd try to move him to the cattle side, where there's still plenty of hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the owners at Fernhill want from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lower costs and no mess-ups. They'd want someone who can make the robots pay for themselves without upsetting the team. Which is a job I'd be good at, honestly.

S1.say: Farms that adapt will do fine and ones that don't will struggle, same as always. Get your people trained.
S1.think: It's good for me, because a manager who can run machines and people is worth more. My worry is the team, and my own patience with learning new systems.
S1.do: Watches what neighbouring big farms buy for a year, then proposes one or two robots for weeding beet. Takes a winter course in farm data if the company pays, and moves an older worker to the cattle side.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a bit tired at the idea of more systems.
S1.quote: He's 50 and he's good, but he'd tell you himself he hates change.
S1.fieldNote: She sees a real upside for herself and says so plainly. Her approach is to let others test first, then present a careful plan. She already has a practical idea for the worker most at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this and we all need to be sensible. I'd say don't panic-sell, don't panic-buy. Governments need to sort out how people get paid, quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think farm managers go too, just a bit later than the workers. If AI can plan and robots can do the work, the owners only need someone to sign things off. I'd give myself two or three years after it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, put off the kitchen we were planning, and pay off more of the house. I'd learn the new systems straight away, even before they're proven, because there's no time to wait. And I'd start looking at jobs on the other side, with the companies selling the robots to farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Kofi would say I'd go quiet, which is what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is quick for someone who waits to see things proven. What would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. I'd have to jump before anyone else had tried it. I hate that. But two years doesn't give you a season to watch the neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything you've said surprised you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd look at working for the robot companies. Ten minutes ago I'd have said no way. But it's probably where a person like me is still useful.

S2.say: Nobody's ready for this, so we all need to be sensible: don't panic-sell, don't panic-buy. Governments need to sort out quickly how people get paid.
S2.think: Farm managers go too, just a bit later than the workers, because owners only need someone to sign things off. I'd give myself two or three years after it lands.
S2.do: Saves harder, delays a planned new kitchen and pays down more of the house. Learns new systems straight away without waiting for proof, and starts looking at jobs with companies selling robots to farms.
S2.quote: But two years doesn't give you a season to watch the neighbours.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline forces her to break her own rule of waiting for proof. Her public line stays sensible while privately she gives herself a deadline. She surprises herself by considering a move to the companies selling the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable if farms and government plan now. I'd say it at the grain group, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to change direction once. Not twice. So I'd want to pick the right direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year watching which farms do it well, then I'd do a proper course, probably in farm systems management, part-time over a year. I'd keep saving a quarter of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But I'd feel I had my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing at the end of year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Either running the robot side at Fernhill or working for whoever supplies them, setting them up on farms. I'd want to know by then which one has a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad grew up on a small farm and left it for the city. He'd probably laugh. He'd say, see, I told you to be a vet.

S3.say: Five years is tight but doable if farms and government plan now. I'd say that at the grain group and mean it.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to change direction once, not twice. So I'd want to pick the right direction.
S3.do: Watches which farms adopt well in the first year, then takes a part-time course in farm systems management. Saves a quarter of her pay and aims to run the robot side of the farm or join a supplier by year three.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to change direction once. Not twice.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits her style: a year of watching, then a committed move. She thinks of the change as one big decision to get right. The family memory of her father leaving farming adds a light, wry note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right, so let's not waste it. Train people, plan the land, sort out how people get paid. Normal, sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is fine for me. I'd have time to try the new systems once they're proven, which is how I like to do things. I'd have time for a second plan if the first didn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big in year one. I'd keep working, take on the robot trials at Fernhill when other farms show they work, and put some savings into a broad share fund, since the companies doing this will make the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Not something I'd talk about much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at 37. Is the long version easier for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Two years was a jump in the dark. Ten is a staircase. I'd also be thinking about kids around then, and I'd want to have it sorted before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be on a farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be near one. Maybe not driving the loader. But I like being out in the beet in October, and I'd hope that's still a job someone does.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do it right, so let's not waste it. Train people, plan the land and sort out how people get paid.
S4.think: Ten years is fine for me, with time to try new systems once they're proven and to make a second plan if the first fails.
S4.do: Keeps working and takes on robot trials at the farm once other farms show they work. Puts some savings into a broad share fund on the view that the companies doing this will make the money.
S4.feel: Quietly uneasy, not something she'd talk about.
S4.quote: Two years was a jump in the dark. Ten is a staircase.
S4.fieldNote: The longer timeline lets her go back to her natural pace. She plans around a possible family later and wants things settled before then. Investing in a share fund is a pragmatic hedge, not an ideological one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because it doesn't give anyone time to see what works. What would help is clear rules early on, how people get paid, what happens to farms, so you can plan instead of guess. And training you don't have to beg your employer for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether we'd still want the food. People like knowing a person grew it. I'd hope a few farms keep people in the fields because customers want them there.

headlineQuote: People like knowing a person grew it.
portrait: Lena Usman is a 27-year-old senior lead at Fernhill, a 700-hectare company farm with wheat, sugar beet and beef cattle, managing six people. She's practical and centrist, uses AI now and then when someone she trusts vouches for it, and lives with her partner Kofi. She's calm in the mild pictures and sees a gain for a manager who can run machines and people. The fast AGI picture makes her anxious because it forces her to jump before anything is proven, while five and ten years let her return to watching first and then making one careful move.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because nobody would have time to see what works.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules set early on how people get paid and what happens to farms, plus training she doesn't have to beg her employer for.
